about: The chapters of two lecture notes, on electrodynamics and, after Lasser (2012), on wave propagation; first those of Prechtl (2010), Vorlesungen über Elektrodynamik, TU Wien, each in a family that colours its cards, with the labs it teaches; then each lab's words and practice questions. Chapter numbers, titles and page ranges are those of the notes' table of contents; equation numbers are the notes' own, checked against the PDF on 1 Nov 2026. Practice answers are worked by hand or, where marked, taken from the worked solutions of the course's exercise collection, the Aufgabensammlung of TU Wien from 2010 (checked against its scanned pages on 1 Nov 2026); tests/unit/labs-data.test.js recomputes each with the core and fails if they disagree.

labs.title: Gauss's law
labs.idea: The electric flux out of any closed surface counts the charge inside it, and nothing else.
labs.law: ∮ n·D dA = ∫ ϱ dV    ∇·D = ϱ

practice.question: A closed surface holds charges of 3 nC, −1 nC and 2 nC; a 5 nC charge sits outside. What electric flux Ψ leaves the surface?
practice.solution: Ψ(∂V) = Q(V) = 3 − 1 + 2 = 4 nC. The charge outside adds nothing.
practice.source: Worked by hand from Tab. 2.1, row 4

equations.note: from the global to the local form

labs.title: No magnetic charge
labs.idea: Magnetic field lines never start or end: as much flux enters any closed surface as leaves it.

practice.question: A closed surface encloses only the north pole of a bar magnet. What magnetic flux leaves it, in Wb?
practice.solution: Zero. Φ(∂V) = 0 for every closed surface: the lines that leave near the pole come back in through the part of the surface that cuts the magnet.
practice.source: Tab. 2.1, row 2, by definition

equations.note: local form: normal B is continuous
so B is a curl: a vector potential exists

labs.title: Induction law
labs.idea: A changing magnetic flux through a loop drives a voltage round it, strongest where the flux changes fastest.
labs.law: ∮ s·E ds = −d/dt ∫ n·B dA    ∇×E = −∂B/∂t

practice.question: A coil of 100 turns, each 0.01 m², sits in a field B̂ sin(ωt) with B̂ = 0.2 T and f = 50 Hz. What is the peak voltage?
practice.source: Worked by hand from Tab. 2.1, row 1

equations.note: local form: tangential E is continuous
for B = B̂ sin ωt through N turns of area A (derived)

labs.title: Ampère–Maxwell law
labs.idea: Current, and a changing electric flux, make a magnetic field that circles it.
labs.law: ∮ s·H ds = ∫ n·J dA + d/dt ∫ n·D dA    ∇×H = J + ∂D/∂t

practice.question: A long straight wire carries 10 A. What is the magnetic field strength H 5 cm from it?
practice.solution: On a circle round the wire H · 2πr = I, so H = 10 A / (2π × 0.05 m) = 31.8 A/m.
practice.source: Worked by hand from Tab. 2.1, row 3

equations.eq: ∮∂A s·H ds = ∫A n·J dA + d/dt ∫A n·D dA

labs.title: Conservation of charge
labs.idea: Charge is never made or lost: the current into a closed surface is the rate the charge inside grows.
labs.law: ∮ n·J dA = −dQ/dt    ∇·J = −∂ϱ/∂t

practice.question: A steady 2 mA flows onto an insulated plate. How long until it holds 1 mC?
practice.solution: dQ/dt = I, so t = Q / I = 1 mC / 2 mA = 0.5 s.
practice.source: Worked by hand from Tab. 2.1, row 5

equations.note: follows from the Ampère–Maxwell and Gauss laws (derived)

labs.title: Material equations
labs.idea: The field E is set by the voltages; how much flux density D, polarisation P and current J it brings depends on the material.
labs.law: D = ε E, ε = ε0 εr, εr = 1 + χ    P = ε0 χ E    J = γ E

practice.question: A material with χ = 3 is in a field of 100 kV/m. What is the flux density D?
practice.solution: εr = 1 + χ = 4, so D = ε0 εr E = 8.854 pC/(V·m) × 4 × 10⁵ V/m = 3.54 µC/m².
practice.source: Worked by hand from (2.37), (2.38)

equations.eq: D = ε0E + P,   H = B/μ0 − M
ε = ε0εr, μ = μ0μr, εr = 1 + χ, μr = 1 + κ

equations.note: Ohm's law in a moving body

labs.title: Poynting vector
labs.idea: Energy flows through the field, not the copper: the power a wire heats with streams in through its surface.
labs.law: S = E × H    ∮ n·(E × H) dA = −∫ J·E dV (static fields)

practice.question: A wire 1 m long and 1 mm in radius carries 3 A with 2 V along it. What is the Poynting vector at its surface?
practice.solution: E = U/l = 2 V/m, H = I/(2πa) = 477.5 A/m, S = E H = 955 W/m². Times the surface 2πal = 6.28 × 10⁻³ m² gives 6 W = U I.
practice.source: Worked by hand from (2.107)

equations.note: static fields: the inflow is the Joule heat

equations.eq: E = U/l,  H = I/(2πa)  ⇒  S·2πal = UI

labs.title: Lorentz force
labs.idea: An electric field pushes a charge along it; a magnetic field pushes only across its motion, so it bends the path but never speeds it up.
labs.law: f = ϱ E + J × B    for one charge: F = q (E + v × B)

practice.question: An electron moves at 10⁶ m/s across a field of 1 mT. What is the radius of its circle?
practice.source: Worked by hand from (2.100)

equations.note: force density on true charges and currents
point charge: ϱ → qδ, J → qvδ (derived)

labs.title: Point charge and potential
labs.idea: A charge raises the potential around it as 1/r; the field points down the potential's slope.
labs.law: ϕ = Q / (4π ε r)    E = −∇ϕ

practice.question: What is the field strength 10 cm from a point charge of 1 nC in vacuum?
practice.source: Worked by hand from (3.13) with E = −∇ϕ

equations.note: fundamental solution of the Laplace operator

labs.title: Laplace equation
labs.idea: Where there is no charge, the potential at each point is the average of its surroundings; the electrodes fix the rest.
labs.law: ∇²ϕ = −ϱ/ε (Poisson)    ∇²ϕ = 0 (Laplace)

practice.question: Two large parallel plates are held at 10 V and 0 V. What is the potential halfway between them?
practice.solution: Between large plates ∇²ϕ = d²ϕ/dx² = 0, so ϕ is linear in x: halfway it is (10 + 0)/2 = 5 V.
practice.source: Worked by hand from (3.9)

labs.title: Electric dipole
labs.idea: Two equal and opposite charges close together: their fields almost cancel, so the potential falls as 1/r² and the field as 1/r³.
labs.law: ϕ = e_r·p / (4π ε0 r²)    E = (3 e_r (e_r·p) − p) / (4π ε0 r³)

practice.question: A dipole of 1 pC·m: what is the potential 10 cm away along its axis?
practice.source: Worked by hand from (5.42)

equations.eq: E_r = 2p cos θ/(4πε0r³),  E_θ = p sin θ/(4πε0r³)

labs.title: Charge relaxation
labs.idea: Charge put inside a conductor does not stay: it dies away exponentially with the time ε/γ and ends up on the surface.
labs.law: ∂ϱ/∂t + (γ/ε) ϱ = 0    ϱ = ϱ0 e^(−t/T_R), T_R = ε/γ

practice.question: Pure water has εr = 80 and γ = 10⁻⁴ S/m. What is its relaxation time?
practice.source: Worked by hand from (3.105)

equations.note: relaxation time and electric Reynolds number

labs.title: Biot–Savart formula
labs.idea: Every short piece of a current adds a little magnetic field; sum the pieces and you have the field of any wire shape.
labs.law: B = μ I / (4π) ∮ s′ × e_R / R² ds′

practice.question: A circular loop of radius 5 cm carries 5 A. What is the flux density at its centre?
practice.solution: Every piece is at R = a and at right angles to e_R, so B = μ0 I / (4π a²) × 2πa = μ0 I / (2a) = 62.8 µT.
practice.source: Worked by hand from (3.144)

equations.note: magnetic scalar potential in current-free regions
on the axis of a circular loop (derived)

labs.title: Skin effect
labs.idea: An alternating field cannot reach deep into a conductor: it dies away and lags within a few skin depths.
labs.law: B = B̂0 e^(−x/δ) cos(ωt − x/δ)    δ = √(2 / (μ ω γ))

practice.question: What is the skin depth of copper (γ = 5.8 × 10⁷ S/m) at 50 Hz?
practice.source: Worked by hand from (4.31)

practice.question: Induction heating (A4.2.8): a cylindrical workpiece (μ = μ0, γ = 10⁷ S/m) sits in a long coil with N′ = 100 turns per metre carrying 600 A (effective) at 100 kHz. What power per unit surface P″ enters it?
practice.source: Course exercise collection, Aufgabensammlung of 2010, A4.2.8; result from its worked solution, p. 205

labs.title: Speed of electromagnetic waves
labs.idea: Maxwell's equations give waves that travel at 1/√(με): in vacuum the speed of light, slower in matter.

practice.question: How fast does an electromagnetic wave travel in a material with εr = 4 and μr = 1?
practice.source: Worked by hand from (5.19)

labs.title: Plane wave
labs.idea: In a free wave E and H stand at right angles to each other and to the direction of travel, in step, their ratio fixed by the medium.
labs.law: H = κ × E / Z    Z = √(μ/ε)    S = E²/Z

practice.question: A plane wave in vacuum has E = 1 V/m. What is H?
practice.source: Worked by hand from (5.70), (5.71)

practice.question: Sunlight (A5.2.5): the mean energy flux density at the ground is about 1 kW/m². Taking a linearly polarised plane wave, what is the amplitude of E?
practice.source: Course exercise collection, Aufgabensammlung of 2010, A5.2.5 (i); result from its worked solution, p. 221

practice.question: Same sunlight, linear polarisation: what is the amplitude of H?
practice.source: Course exercise collection, Aufgabensammlung of 2010, A5.2.5 (i); result from its worked solution, p. 221

practice.question: Same sunlight, now circularly polarised: what is |E|?
practice.solution: With circular polarisation |E| = Z0|H| is constant and S = ⟨S⟩, so E = √(Z0 S) = 614 V/m (and H = 1.63 A/m).
practice.source: Course exercise collection, Aufgabensammlung of 2010, A5.2.5 (ii); result from its worked solution, p. 222

practice.question: Broadcast signal (A5.2.6): a transmitter radiates 100 kW at 100 MHz. Treating it as an isotropic point source with circular polarisation, what is the field amplitude 10 km away?
practice.source: Course exercise collection, Aufgabensammlung of 2010, A5.2.6; result from its worked solution, p. 222

labs.title: Hertz dipole
labs.idea: A short antenna radiates across its axis, not along it, and the power it sends out grows with the square of its length in wavelengths.
labs.law: P = R_S I²    R_S = (2π/3) (l/λ)² Z0

practice.question: A short dipole is a tenth of a wavelength long. What is its radiation resistance?
practice.source: Worked by hand from (5.53)

practice.question: Dipole antenna (A5.1.3): far from it the field is E = (U/r) sin θ cos(ωt − kr) e_θ, with U = 100 V. What mean power does it radiate?
practice.solution: ⟨S⟩ = U² sin²θ / (2 μ0c0 r²); over a sphere P = (πU²/(μ0c0)) ∫ sin³θ dθ = (4π/3) U²/Z0 = 111 W.
practice.source: Course exercise collection, Aufgabensammlung of 2010, A5.1.3; result from its worked solution, p. 215

equations.note: Hertz vector of an oscillating dipole

labs.title: Transmission line
labs.idea: On a line, voltage and current travel as waves; a load equal to the wave impedance swallows them, any other load sends some back.
labs.law: Z_W = √(Z′/Y′)    γ = √(Y′Z′)    Z′ = R′ + jωL′, Y′ = G′ + jωC′

practice.question: A lossless line has L′ = 250 nH/m and C′ = 100 pF/m. What is its wave impedance?
practice.source: Worked by hand from (5.110)

practice.question: TEM wave impedance (A5.3.1 a): an air-filled coaxial line with D = 10 d. What is Z_W?
practice.source: Course exercise collection, Aufgabensammlung of 2010, A5.3.1 (a); result from its worked solution, p. 235

practice.question: (A5.3.1 b) A two-wire line in air, wire spacing D = 10 d, (d/D)² ≪ 1. What is Z_W?
practice.solution: C′ ≈ πε/ln(2D/d), L′ ≈ (μ/π) ln(2D/d), so Z_W ≈ Z0 ln(2D/d)/π = 376.7 Ω × ln 20 / π = 359 Ω.
practice.source: Course exercise collection, Aufgabensammlung of 2010, A5.3.1 (b); result from its worked solution, p. 235

practice.question: (A5.3.1 c) A strip line in air, strips b = 10 a wide at spacing a. What is Z_W?
practice.solution: C′ ≈ εb/a, L′ ≈ μa/b, so Z_W ≈ Z0 a/b = 37.7 Ω.
practice.source: Course exercise collection, Aufgabensammlung of 2010, A5.3.1 (c); result from its worked solution, p. 235

equations.eq: U(z) = [Z_A cosh γ(l−z) + Z_W sinh γ(l−z)] / [Z_A cosh γl + Z_W sinh γl] · U(0)

equations.note: input impedance of an open lossless line

labs.title: Polarisation
labs.idea: Two field components across the wave, out of step, make the tip of E trace a line, a circle or an ellipse.
labs.law: e_x = E1 cos ωt    e_y = E2 cos(ωt + ψ)    ellipticity a/b

equations.eq: e_x(0,t) = E1 cos ωt,  e_y(0,t) = E2 cos(ωt + ψ)
ψ = ∓90°, E1 = E2  ⇒  e_x² + e_y² = E²
equations.note: circular: right-hand for −90°, clockwise seen along the wave
a, b the half axes of the ellipse

equations.eq: e_x(z,0) = E cos kz,  e_y(z,0) = ±E sin kz
equations.note: at a fixed time: a screw in space

practice.question: E1 = 2 V/m, E2 = 1 V/m, ψ = 90°. What is the ellipticity in dB?
practice.solution: With ψ = 90° the ellipse is upright with half axes a = 2 and b = 1, so 20 log(2/1) = 6.02 dB.
practice.source: Worked by hand from Lasser (2012), Fig. 3.4

labs.title: Plane wave in a lossy medium
labs.idea: Conductivity turns the permittivity complex; one formula then covers everything from glass to copper.
labs.law: δ = ε(1 − js), s = σ/(εω)    γ = α + jβ = jω√(μδ)

equations.note: loss tangent: quality factor of the medium, loss angle

equations.eq: E = Ê e^(−γ·r),  γ = α + jβ
equations.note: plane wave with complex propagation constant
good conductor: the skin depth of Prechtl (2010), (4.31) (derived)

practice.question: Sea water (εr = 80, σ = 4 S/m) at 1 MHz: at what depth has the field fallen to 1/e?
practice.source: Worked by hand from Lasser (2012), p. 38

labs.title: Reflection and refraction
labs.idea: At a boundary a wave splits into a reflected and a transmitted part; how much depends on the angle and on whether E lies in the plane of incidence.
labs.law: sin Θ1 / sin Θ2 = n2/n1    Γ_TE, Γ_TM (Fresnel)    tan Θ_B = n2/n1

equations.eq: Γ_TM = (n² cos Θ1 − √(n² − sin²Θ1)) / (n² cos Θ1 + √(n² − sin²Θ1))
T_TM = 2n cos Θ1 / (n² cos Θ1 + √(n² − sin²Θ1))

equations.note: Brewster angle; none in the TE case
total reflection beyond Θ_c, from Snell's law with Θ2 = 90° (derived)

practice.question: At what angle does TM light pass from air into glass (n = 1.5) without reflection?
practice.source: Worked by hand from Lasser (2012), p. 46

labs.title: Rectangular waveguide
labs.idea: A metal tube carries a wave only above a cutoff frequency set by its width; between the first two cutoffs exactly one mode runs.
labs.law: κ² = (mπ/a)² + (nπ/b)² = ω²εμ − k_z²    λ_G = 2a for TE10

equations.note: for TE and TM modes alike
cutoff wavelength of the fundamental mode TE10

practice.question: What is the TE10 cutoff frequency of a WR-90 guide, a = 22.86 mm?
practice.source: Worked by hand from Lasser (2012), p. 66

labs.title: Microstrip line
labs.idea: On a circuit board the field runs partly in air and partly in the substrate; the wave sees an average of the two.
labs.law: ε_eff = 1 + q(ε_r − 1)    Z_L = Z_L,0/√ε_eff    λ = λ0/√ε_eff

equations.note: Z_L,0 the same line in air

practice.question: A very narrow strip on FR-4 (εr = 4.4), q = 0.5. What is ε_eff?
practice.source: Worked by hand from Lasser (2012), p. 96

practice.question: Exercise 14: a 50 Ω microstrip at 1680 MHz on epoxy (εr = 4.325, h = 1.6 mm) ends its iteration at w = 3.2 mm and ε_eff = 3.33. What is the wavelength on the line?
practice.source: Wave propagation exercise collection (Übungsteil, 5th edition, October 2011), exercise 14; result from its worked solution, p. 32

practice.question: Same line: what filling factor q goes with ε_eff = 3.33 on εr = 4.325?
practice.solution: ε_eff = 1 + q(εr − 1), so q = (3.33 − 1)/(4.325 − 1) = 0.70; the nomogram gives about 0.7.
practice.source: Wave propagation exercise collection (Übungsteil, 5th edition, October 2011), exercise 14; result from its worked solution, p. 32

labs.title: Fresnel zones
labs.idea: A radio link needs more than a clear line of sight: the ellipsoid of paths up to half a wavelength longer must stay free too.
labs.law: detour = λ/2 on the 1st Fresnel ellipsoid    r = √(λ d1 d2 / d)

equations.note: the 1st Fresnel ellipsoid: detour of half a wavelength, phase shift π
the detour at height r above the line of sight (derived)
inner and outer halves of the 1st zone

practice.question: The notes' exercise: a radio link of d = 50 km at λ = 5 cm. How wide is the 1st Fresnel zone at most?
practice.solution: At mid-path d1 = d2 = 25 km: r = √(λ d1 d2/d) = √(0.05 m × 12.5 km) = 25 m, so the diameter is 50 m.
practice.source: Lasser (2012), exercise on p. 107; the notes give D = 50 m

labs.title: Link budget
labs.idea: A radio link is an account in decibels: transmit power, plus the gains, minus the free-space loss, against the receiver's minimum.
labs.law: P_e = P_s G_s G_e (λ/(4πd))²    L_ISO = −20 log(λ/(4πd))

equations.note: power flux density of an antenna with gain G
with antenna areas instead of gains

equations.eq: P_e = P_s + G_s − L_ISO + G_e (in dB)

practice.question: What is the basic transmission loss L_ISO at 1 GHz over 1 km?
practice.source: Worked by hand from Lasser (2012), (12.10)

practice.question: Exercise 26, secondary radar: an interrogation at 1030 MHz from a 10 dBi antenna to an aircraft 100 km away with a 3 dBi antenna, receiver 200 K and 1 MHz, k = 10⁻²³ Ws/K. What transmit power gives 20 dB SNR in the aircraft?
practice.source: Wave propagation exercise collection (Übungsteil, 5th edition, October 2011), exercise 26, p. 50; the collection prints no number, answer worked by hand

labs.title: Radar equation
labs.idea: A radar hears its own echo: the wave travels out and back, so the echo falls with the fourth power of range.
labs.law: P_e/P_s = σ G² (λ/4π)² / (4π d⁴)

equations.eq: P_e = T_e A_e = P_s G_s σ λ² G_e / ((4πd²)² 4π)

equations.note: flat plate square to the beam

practice.question: What is the radar cross-section of a metal sphere 1 m in radius (r ≫ λ)?
practice.source: Worked by hand from Lasser (2012), (12.19)

practice.question: Exercise 22: a retroreflector of 2 m² with aperture efficiency 0.6, at 1.5 GHz. What is its radar cross-section?
practice.solution: σ = A_w G = 4π A_w²/λ² with A_w = 0.6 × 2 m² = 1.2 m² and λ = 0.2 m: 4π × 1.44 / 0.04 = 452 m².
practice.source: Wave propagation exercise collection (Übungsteil, 5th edition, October 2011), exercise 22; result from its worked solution, p. 44

practice.question: The same retroreflector at 15 GHz?
practice.solution: Ten times the frequency, λ² a hundredth: σ = 45 240 m². A retroreflector gains with frequency as fast as the radar loses.
practice.source: Wave propagation exercise collection (Übungsteil, 5th edition, October 2011), exercise 22; result from its worked solution, p. 44

practice.question: Exercise 21: the Moon as a passive reflector (d = 380 000 km, D_M = 3476 km, reflection coefficient 0.065) between two stations with 7 m dishes (efficiency 0.7), T = 190 K, B = 100 Hz, at 1.5 GHz. What transmit power gives 20 dB SNR, the beam lighting the whole Moon?
practice.solution: P_E = 100 k T B = 2.62 × 10⁻¹⁷ W; A_e = πD²w/4 = 26.9 m²; σ = π D_M²/4 · r = 617 × 10⁹ m²; EIRP = P_E (4πd²)² / (σ A_e) = 5.19 MW; G_s = 4πA_e/λ² = 8460, so P_s = 613 W.
practice.source: Wave propagation exercise collection (Übungsteil, 5th edition, October 2011), exercise 21; result from its worked solution, pp. 42–43

practice.question: Same link at 15 GHz, where the beam (about 1300 km wide) is narrower than the Moon. What transmit power is needed now?
practice.solution: All the power reaches the Moon, which reflects the share r: P_E = P_s r A_e / (4πd²), so P_s = 2.62 × 10⁻¹⁷ W × 4π(3.8 × 10⁸ m)² / (0.065 × 26.9 m²) = 27 W.
practice.source: Wave propagation exercise collection (Übungsteil, 5th edition, October 2011), exercise 21; result from its worked solution, p. 43

practice.question: Exercise 26: an airport primary radar, P_s = 44 dBW, G = 40 dBi, at 2.8 GHz; aircraft σ = 100 m²; receiver 160 K, 200 MHz, k = 10⁻²³ Ws/K. What is the largest range for an SNR of 13 dB?
practice.solution: Noise k T B = 3.2 × 10⁻¹³ W = −124.9 dBW, so the echo must reach −111.9 dBW. From (12.17) in dB: 40 log d = 44 + 80 + 20 + 20 log 0.107 − 30 log 4π + 111.9 = 203.5, d = 122 km.
practice.source: Wave propagation exercise collection (Übungsteil, 5th edition, October 2011), exercise 26, p. 50; the collection prints no number, answer worked by hand

labs.title: Fading in space
labs.idea: Two waves crossing at an angle build a pattern of strong and weak field; a moving receiver drives through its holes.
labs.law: λ_S = λ / (2 sin(φ/2))    depth (A1 − A2)/(A1 + A2)    Δf_D = −(v/λ) cos γ

equations.note: the wave after a path d
the path grows at speed v
moving at an angle γ to the wave
the beat of two Doppler-shifted carriers
distance between fades across the pattern of two waves at angle φ (derived, as in exercise 24)
fade depth: the weakest field against the strongest (derived)

practice.question: Exercise 24: at 900 MHz the signal arrives from two directions 45° apart, 2 dB different. How far apart are the fades across the pattern?
practice.source: Wave propagation exercise collection (Übungsteil, 5th edition, October 2011), exercise 24; result from its worked solution, p. 46

practice.question: The car drives across the pattern at 60 km/h. How many fades per second?
practice.solution: v/λ_S = 16.67 m/s / 0.435 m = 38.3 per second; driving along the stripes it would be zero.
practice.source: Wave propagation exercise collection (Übungsteil, 5th edition, October 2011), exercise 24; result from its worked solution, p. 47

practice.question: How deep are the fades, in dB, when the two waves differ by 2 dB?
practice.source: Wave propagation exercise collection (Übungsteil, 5th edition, October 2011), exercise 24; result from its worked solution, p. 47

practice.question: The notes' exercise: how large is the Doppler shift at 900 MHz and 60 km/h?
practice.source: Lasser (2012), exercise on p. 150; worked by hand from (13.11)

labs.title: Frequency-selective fading
labs.idea: Echoes arriving later cut regular notches into the channel's spectrum; how far apart they lie decides whether a signal is narrowband or wideband.
labs.law: |H(jω)| = √(A1² + A2² + 2A1A2 cos ωΔτ)    notches every 1/Δτ

equations.note: the delays of the two paths

equations.eq: h(τ) = A1 δ(τ − τ1) + A2 δ(τ − τ2)
|H(jω)| = √(A1² + A2² + 2A1A2 cos ωΔτ),  Δτ = τ2 − τ1

equations.note: strong ISI from half a symbol of delay, the collection's working rule

practice.question: Exercise 25: indoors the longest and shortest paths differ by Δτ = 20 ns. How far apart are the notches in frequency?
practice.solution: ΔB = 1/Δτ = 1/20 ns = 50 MHz: a 10 MHz channel is five times narrower and sees at most one notch.
practice.source: Wave propagation exercise collection (Übungsteil, 5th edition, October 2011), exercise 25; result from its worked solution, p. 48

practice.question: Above what symbol rate must one expect strong intersymbol interference?
practice.solution: Strong ISI from a delay of half a symbol: the shortest symbol is 2Δτ = 40 ns, so at most 25 MBd.
practice.source: Wave propagation exercise collection (Übungsteil, 5th edition, October 2011), exercise 25; result from its worked solution, p. 48
